description: A team of passionate innovators and problem-solvers driven by curiosity, creativity, and technology. We aim to turn ideas into impactful solutions by exploring space, leveraging NASA's open data, and pushing the boundaries of innovation.
summary:
MISSIONFORGE is an educational web game, built for the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge, that teaches how space missions are designed. Players start from a science question, turn it into measurable requirements, and assemble a 3D spacecraft from a parts catalogue. As they work, they watch mass, power, propulsion, data, communications and cost budgets update together. They clear engineering readiness gates, fly a deterministic simulation with anomalies and operator decisions, and finish with a debrief that explains why the mission succeeded or failed.
It meets the challenge by making systems-engineering trade-offs playable. Every choice has visible consequences: a better antenna fixes the link but costs power and money, and observing less brings home data but less science. A Python engine computes every result, so the interface never invents numbers. Each value is labelled source-backed, derived, gameplay estimate or not modelled. The asteroid scenario uses NASA JPL’s mission-design data through the backend, falling back to a clearly labelled offline snapshot.
This matters because real mission design rarely has one best answer. MISSIONFORGE helps students and the public understand the coupled decisions behind spaceflight, and it never presents itself as a real flight-design tool.
details:
MISSIONFORGE is a playable mission-design console. Players pick a scenario: an asteroid rendezvous, a lunar polar orbiter, or an Earth-observation satellite. They turn science objectives into measurable requirements and build a 3D spacecraft from a parts catalogue. Every change becomes a new design revision that a Python engine re-analyses for mass, power, propulsion, data, communications and cost. Players then clear readiness gates, fly a deterministic simulation with anomalies and operator decisions, and finish with a debrief that explains what happened and why.

The game makes engineering trade-offs visible: a stronger antenna fixes the link but costs mass, power and money. Every value is labelled as source-backed, derived, a gameplay estimate or not modelled, and a high score never hides a failed check. The app runs offline on an ordinary laptop and works with a keyboard, at phone width and without 3D support. We want students and the public to learn that mission design rarely has one best answer, only defensible compromises.

We built it in Python (FastAPI, Pydantic) and TypeScript (Next.js, React, Tailwind, Zustand, Recharts), with the 3D view made in Three.js. More than 1,300 automated tests check it, and asteroid targets come from NASA JPL’s mission-design API through the server, with an offline fallback.

Our main priorities were scientific honesty, reproducible results, responsible use of JPL data, and accessibility. With limited hackathon time, we documented clearly what the game does not model rather than faking it.
